subtasks.title: DECIDE: do we persist the face template at all, or verify-and-delete?
subtasks.description:
THE SINGLE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE DECISION IN THIS ENTIRE PROJECT. Make it before writing any of the compliance documents, because every document's content depends on the answer.

OPTION A — VERIFY AND DELETE. Capture the image, run the match against the government ID, delete both the image and the derived template within minutes. Persist only a boolean ('verified'), a timestamp, and a non-biometric audit reference.
What this buys us:
- Illinois BIPA: the written-retention-schedule duty becomes trivial (schedule = 'deleted on completion of verification'), and the per-scan damages base is one scan per user rather than an ongoing stored template.
- Maryland MODPA: the strict-necessity problem largely dissolves. Retention is a separate processing activity that must independently be strictly necessary, and ongoing storage after verification is very hard to justify. Deleting removes the argument.
- Washington RCW 19.375: the statute's duties hinge on 'enrolling' a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose. If nothing is enrolled, the trigger arguably never fires.
- California §1798.150: statutory damages of $100–$750 per consumer per incident need a breach of stored biometric data. No stored template, nothing to breach. At 500k users a breach is a $50m–$375m statutory exposure; this option zeroes it.
- Vendor risk: if the IDV vendor never retains either, our exposure through them drops correspondingly.

OPTION B — PERSIST THE TEMPLATE. Only justified if Product has a concrete requirement: biometric re-authentication at login, duplicate/multi-account detection, or chargeback and fraud dispute evidence.
What this costs us: the full weight of all five Tier 1/2 regimes simultaneously, a real strict-necessity problem in Maryland, a real breach-exposure problem in California, and a materially larger BIPA damages base. It is a legitimate business choice but it must be a deliberate, documented one.

IF OPTION B, RECORD IN WRITING (this record is itself a compliance artifact):
1. The specific business purpose retention serves.
2. Why a non-biometric alternative (device binding, document-only re-verification, phone/email step-up, behavioural signals) will not achieve it.
3. The retention period and the deletion trigger.
4. Whether the template is encrypted at rest — note that California's private right of action reaches only NONENCRYPTED, NONREDACTED data, so encryption at rest is a statutory defence, not merely hygiene, and it also generally keeps us outside the breach-notification triggers in most states.

HARD RULE REGARDLESS OF OPTION, NOT NEGOTIABLE: never train, fine-tune, or evaluate any model on user face data collected for verification. FTC Act §5 remedies include algorithmic disgorgement — deletion of the model trained on improperly collected face data. That is the one outcome we cannot pay our way out of. Put it in the vendor contract too.

Output: a one-paragraph written decision, dated, with the four items above if Option B. Attach it here.

subtasks.title: DECIDE: launch in Illinois, geofence it, or delay it
subtasks.description:
GO/NO-GO CALL. Only a human can make this one — it is a risk-appetite and revenue trade-off, not a research question.

WHY ILLINOIS IS SINGLED OUT. BIPA is the only biometric statute in the country combining (a) a private right of action, (b) liquidated statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation and $5,000 per reckless or intentional violation, (c) no requirement to prove any actual injury — a bare procedural violation confers standing under Rosenbach, and (d) mandatory attorneys' fees, which is what funds the plaintiffs' bar. Illinois is roughly 95% of our total nationwide biometric litigation exposure. Practically every large biometric settlement in the US has been a BIPA case.

THE 2024 AMENDMENT (SB 2979) HELPS, BUT LESS THAN THE HEADLINES SUGGEST. It resolved Cothron by making repeated collection from the same person by the same method a SINGLE violation rather than one per scan. That converts per-scan accrual into per-person accrual. It does NOT cap class size. At 50,000 Illinois users, $1,000 per person is still $50m of theoretical exposure, and one defective consent screen is a single defect replicated across the whole class. The amendment also expressly permits electronic signatures for the written release, which is what makes a compliant in-app flow possible at all.

THE OPTIONS:
1. LAUNCH WITH A FULLY BIPA-COMPLIANT FLOW. Viable, and the requirements are well-documented. Requires all four pre-launch documents finished and counsel-reviewed, and no shortcuts on the written release. Highest revenue, highest residual risk, and the risk is concentrated in execution quality.
2. GEOFENCE ILLINOIS AT LAUNCH. Block Illinois residents from the biometric flow (not necessarily from the product — consider a manual or document-only verification path for IL users). Buys time to get the flow right and validated elsewhere. Costs Illinois revenue (~4% of US population) and adds an alternate-path engineering cost. Note geofencing is imperfect — VPNs and travellers — so it mitigates rather than eliminates.
3. DELAY LAUNCH until the flow is counsel-approved everywhere. Safest, slowest.

MY READ, FOR WHAT IT IS WORTH: option 1 is defensible IF AND ONLY IF the written release and the published retention schedule are both genuinely done and reviewed by counsel who has litigated BIPA. If there is any pressure to ship before those are finished, option 2 is the cheap insurance, because the failure mode in Illinois is not a fine — it is a class action with fee-shifting.

Do not make this call off my research alone. Pair it with the counsel review subtask.

subtasks.title: Book a scoping call with privacy counsel who has actually litigated BIPA
subtasks.description:
Engage outside counsel to review and sign off before launch. Specify BIPA LITIGATION experience, not general privacy advisory experience — the defence bar that has actually tried these cases prices and scopes this very differently from a generalist.

BRING TO THE CALL: the attached report from the parent task, the retention decision, and the draft consent screen copy.

THE SIX QUESTIONS TO PUT TO THEM — these are the genuinely unsettled points my research could not resolve, and they are where the money is:
1. Does our face-scan-plus-ID-match flow create a BIPA 'biometric identifier' or 'biometric information' as we have actually built it? Confirm the vendor's processing is also covered and that our §15(b) written release names the vendor as a recipient.
2. WASHINGTON: does a face scan used purely for identity verification, revealing nothing about health, constitute 'consumer health data' under MHMDA? MHMDA's umbrella definition requires a link to health status, but biometric data is an enumerated category and plaintiffs are arguing per se coverage. Unresolved, and MHMDA has a private right of action. Get a view on whether we need the separate consumer-health-data privacy policy.
3. MARYLAND: is capturing the scan 'strictly necessary to provide a specific product or service requested by the consumer' for our product? Consent is not a defence in Maryland. Separately: is RETAINING it strictly necessary? These are two different questions with two different answers.
4. TEXAS CUBI: confirm our retention satisfies 'within a reasonable time, not to exceed one year after the purpose for collection expires,' and confirm no sale (Texas also requires a specific posted notice if biometric data is sold — we intend never to trigger it).
5. COLORADO HB 24-1130: confirm we are not conditioning provision of the service on biometric consent in a way the statute prohibits, given verification is a gate to signup. This is the most direct legal conflict with our product design and I could not resolve it from public sources.
6. Do the NYC Biometric Identifier Information Law ('commercial establishment' = physical premises) and the Portland face-recognition ban ('place of public accommodation') reach a mobile app? My read is no on both, but neither has been tested against an app and both carry private rights of action.

Ask for a written memo, and ask specifically for the Illinois go/no-go recommendation. Also ask whether our EO/tech E&O policy covers BIPA statutory damages — many policies now carry express biometric exclusions, and finding that out after a claim is the expensive way.

subtasks.title: Draft the biometric consent screen — copy is written below, needs counsel review
subtasks.description:
DRAFT COPY IS BELOW AND READY TO HAND TO COUNSEL. Do not ship it unreviewed — I am not a lawyer, and this screen is the single artifact most likely to be exhibit A in a BIPA complaint.

DESIGN REQUIREMENTS, each traceable to a specific statute:
- Presented BEFORE any capture, on its own screen. Not in the Terms of Service. Not in the privacy policy. Not bundled with anything else. (BIPA §15(b), which requires a written release EXECUTED BY the subject; Colorado; Washington.)
- An unchecked checkbox plus a distinct affirmative action. No pre-ticked boxes, no 'by continuing you agree', no consent inferred from proceeding. (Every opt-in state; MHMDA requires a clear affirmative act that is freely given, specific, informed, opt-in, voluntary and unambiguous.)
- Electronic signature is expressly permitted for the BIPA written release under the 2024 SB 2979 amendment. Capture and STORE the consent artifact: user ID, timestamp, the exact version of the text shown, and the affirmative action taken. If we cannot later prove which words a specific user saw on a specific date, we cannot prove consent. Version the copy and keep every version forever.
- Sensitive-data notice must be surfaced ON SCREEN, not linked — Iowa and Utah require notice to be 'presented' and both statutes distinguish it from the general privacy policy.
- A refusal path that is not a dead end (see the Colorado subtask).

--- DRAFT COPY, v0.1 ---
Heading: Verify your identity with a face scan

Body:
To confirm you are who you say you are, we will take a short video selfie and compare it to the photo ID you provided.

What we collect: an image of your face and a mathematical representation of your facial features (a 'face template'). This is biometric data.

Why we collect it: to verify your identity when you create your account, and to prevent fraudulent and duplicate accounts.

Who receives it: [VENDOR LEGAL NAME], the identity verification provider that performs the match on our behalf. We do not sell, lease, trade, or otherwise profit from your biometric data, and we never will. We do not use your face data to train or improve any facial recognition model.

How long we keep it: [IF VERIFY-AND-DELETE: 'Your face image and face template are permanently deleted within [N] minutes of completing verification. We keep only the fact that you were verified and the date.'] [IF RETAINING: 'We keep your face template for [PERIOD], and permanently delete it within [N] days of whichever happens first: the purpose for collecting it is satisfied, or [N] years after your last interaction with us.']

Your choices: You can decline. If you decline, you can still create an account and verify your identity by [ALTERNATIVE METHOD]. You can withdraw your consent and request deletion at any time at [LINK] or by emailing [ADDRESS] — it is as easy to withdraw as it was to give.

Our full biometric data retention and destruction policy is available at [LINK].

Checkbox (unchecked by default): I have read the above and I consent to [COMPANY] and [VENDOR] collecting, using, and storing my biometric data as described.

Buttons: [Scan my face]  [Verify another way]
--- END DRAFT ---

OPEN ITEMS FOR COUNSEL / PRODUCT TO FILL: vendor legal name; the retention branch (depends on the retain-vs-delete decision); the alternative verification method; whether we need Washington-specific separate consent for any SHARING beyond the vendor performing the match; and whether a distinct MHMDA consent is required if we conclude MHMDA applies.

Deliverable: final copy, versioned, with a screenshot of the implemented screen stored alongside it.

subtasks.title: Write the public biometric data retention and destruction schedule
subtasks.description:
A SEPARATE, PUBLICLY AVAILABLE WRITTEN DOCUMENT. This is a standalone statutory requirement and one of the two most commonly pleaded BIPA counts — it is also one of the easiest to satisfy, which is what makes failing to do it so costly.

STATUTORY BASIS:
- BIPA §15(a): a private entity in possession of biometric identifiers must develop a WRITTEN policy, MADE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC, establishing a retention schedule and guidelines for permanently destroying biometric identifiers when the initial purpose for collection has been satisfied OR within 3 YEARS of the individual's last interaction with the entity, WHICHEVER OCCURS FIRST. Note 'whichever occurs first' — the 3 years is an outer ceiling, not an allowance.
- Texas CUBI: destroy within a REASONABLE TIME, and in any event NOT LATER THAN ONE YEAR after the purpose for collection expires. Texas is stricter than Illinois. Drafting to Texas satisfies Illinois automatically.
- Washington RCW 19.375: retain no longer than reasonably necessary to provide the service, prevent fraud, or comply with a court order.
- Maryland MODPA: retention must independently be STRICTLY NECESSARY. This is the binding constraint if we retain at all.

WHAT THE DOCUMENT MUST CONTAIN:
1. What biometric data we collect and the specific purpose.
2. The retention period, stated as a definite period — not 'as long as necessary', which is exactly the language plaintiffs attack.
3. The destruction trigger, expressed as 'whichever occurs first' between purpose-satisfied and the outer limit.
4. The destruction method, and confirmation it reaches BACKUPS, LOGS, and the VENDOR's systems. Deletion that leaves the template in a backup snapshot or a vendor's cache is not destruction.
5. Who is accountable for executing it.

DRAFT TO THE STRICTEST STANDARD AND PUBLISH ONE SCHEDULE NATIONWIDE. Do not write fifty. Recommended if we retain: destroy on satisfaction of purpose or within one year of last interaction, whichever comes first — this clears Texas's one-year ceiling, is well inside BIPA's three years, and is defensible in Maryland. If we go verify-and-delete, the schedule is a short paragraph and this whole task takes fifteen minutes.

THE PART EVERYONE GETS WRONG: writing the policy is not compliance. The schedule must actually EXECUTE. Build the deletion job, monitor it, and alarm on failure. A published schedule we demonstrably do not follow is worse than no schedule, because it converts a technical violation into a deceptive-practice claim under UDAP statutes in all 50 states — and most of those have private rights of action.

Deliverable: published page at a stable URL, linked from the consent screen and the privacy policy, plus a ticket for the automated deletion job and its monitoring.

subtasks.title: Decide and build the non-biometric verification fallback path
subtasks.description:
REQUIRED, NOT OPTIONAL, AND IT IS A PRODUCT DECISION WITH A LEGAL DEADLINE.

WHY: Colorado HB 24-1130 prohibits conditioning the provision of a service on biometric consent except in narrow enumerated circumstances. Consent that is a precondition to using the product at all is vulnerable to being characterised as not freely given — which is the standard MHMDA and the opt-in states apply. Maryland compounds it: if there is a workable non-biometric way to verify, that is direct evidence the face scan is not 'strictly necessary'.

Note the genuine tension, which is worth naming out loud: building a good fallback strengthens our Colorado and consent-validity position but weakens our Maryland strict-necessity argument. Discuss with counsel. The resolution is usually that a fallback is still the right call, because Colorado's prohibition is explicit while Maryland's necessity test is fact-dependent — but make the call knowingly rather than by accident.

OPTIONS TO EVALUATE:
- Document-only review (ID upload with human or automated review, no face match). Most common answer. Slower, costs more per check.
- Knowledge-based verification against credit-header or public-record data.
- Micro-deposit or bank-account linking, if we are financial.
- Manual review queue via support. Cheapest to build, does not scale, fine at launch volumes.

DECIDE: which path, what it costs per verification, what the SLA is, and who staffs it.
THEN BUILD: the 'Verify another way' button on the consent screen must actually go somewhere. A refusal path that dead-ends into 'you cannot use this app' is the specific failure Colorado targets.

Also confirm the fallback is genuinely available to users who withdraw consent later, not only to users who decline at signup — withdrawal must be as easy as consent was to give, and withdrawal that silently bricks the account is a problem.

subtasks.title: Get biometric covenants into the IDV vendor contract / DPA
subtasks.description:
OUR VENDOR'S NON-COMPLIANCE BECOMES OUR LIABILITY. Under Washington MHMDA a processor that processes outside the contract's instructions BECOMES A REGULATED ENTITY and inherits full liability — and we remain on the hook to the consumer regardless. BIPA plaintiffs routinely name both the app and the biometrics vendor.

GET THESE IN WRITING FROM [VENDOR] BEFORE LAUNCH:
1. VENDOR RETENTION. Exactly how long do they keep the image and the template after returning the match result? Get a number, in the contract, not in a sales email. Push for zero-retention or minutes. Many IDV vendors default to keeping data for their own model improvement — that default is unacceptable.
2. NO TRAINING. Express prohibition on using our users' face data to train, fine-tune, evaluate, or improve any model, theirs or a third party's. FTC Act §5 remedies include algorithmic disgorgement — deletion of the trained model. This is the clause that protects us from the one remedy we cannot pay our way out of.
3. NO SALE, NO SHARING, NO ONWARD DISCLOSURE for value. Needed for the NYC absolute sale ban (no consent exception; $5,000 per intentional violation with a private right of action), Maryland's outright ban on selling sensitive data (consent does not override), and to keep us out of Texas's 'NOTICE: We may sell your biometric personal data' posting requirement.
4. DELETION ON DEMAND, propagating to backups, within a committed SLA. We cannot honour deletion rights in Washington, Colorado, California and elsewhere if the vendor cannot delete on our instruction. Ask specifically about backup retention windows — that is where deletion promises quietly fail.
5. SUBPROCESSORS. Full list, plus notice and objection rights on change. We must name recipients in the BIPA §15(b) release, so we need to know who they are and be told when that changes.
6. SECURITY. Encryption at rest and in transit. California's private right of action reaches only NONENCRYPTED, NONREDACTED data, so vendor-side encryption is a statutory defence for us, and it generally keeps us outside most states' breach-notification triggers.
7. BREACH NOTIFICATION to us within 24–48 hours, with cooperation obligations. Most state breach statutes now include biometric data; our clock starts when they tell us.
8. INDEMNITY for biometric privacy claims arising from their processing, and confirm their insurance actually covers biometric statutory damages. Check for a biometric exclusion — they have become common. An indemnity from an uninsured vendor against a nine-figure BIPA class is decorative.
9. AUDIT / evidence rights: SOC 2 report, and the right to verify deletion actually happened.

While you are at it, check OUR OWN tech E&O / cyber policy for a biometric exclusion. Ask the broker directly and in writing: 'does this policy cover BIPA statutory damages and defence costs?'

subtasks.title: Write the DPIA, with a dedicated Maryland strict-necessity section
subtasks.description:
A data protection impact assessment is MANDATORY for processing sensitive data under essentially every comprehensive state privacy law, and biometric data is sensitive data in all of them. One assessment covers all states — do not write twenty.

STANDARD CONTENTS: the processing described; categories of data; purposes; the benefits to us, to consumers and to the public; the risks to consumers; the safeguards that mitigate those risks; and the conclusion that benefits outweigh residual risk. Reviewed and dated, refreshed when the processing materially changes.

*** THE SECTION OFF-THE-SHELF TEMPLATES DO NOT HAVE, AND THE REASON THIS TASK EXISTS ***
Maryland MODPA requires the assessment to include a NECESSITY ASSESSMENT for all sensitive data processing — because in Maryland consent is not a lawful basis and the only question is whether the processing is STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide or maintain a specific product or service the consumer requested. Your vendor's DPIA template will not have this. Write it explicitly:
- What specific product or service did the consumer request?
- Why is a face scan strictly necessary to provide THAT product, as opposed to merely useful, cheaper, or better at reducing fraud? Be honest here; a self-serving answer is worse than no answer, because this document is discoverable.
- What non-biometric alternatives were considered, and on what concrete grounds were they rejected? (See the fallback subtask — these two documents must tell the same story.)
- Separately and explicitly: is RETENTION strictly necessary, and for how long? Capture and retention are two different processing activities requiring two different necessity findings. Once a user is verified, ongoing storage of the template is the hardest thing in this whole project to justify.

Also cover, since one document should serve everywhere: Colorado's sensitive-data and sensitive-data-inference rules and its delete-or-anonymise-on-withdrawal duty; Washington MHMDA if we conclude it applies; profiling and automated decision-making, since our face match IS an automated decision affecting access to a paid service, which several states treat as a heightened-risk activity requiring its own assessment.

FREE WIN WHILE YOU ARE IN HERE: Tennessee provides an AFFIRMATIVE DEFENCE for a written privacy program that reasonably conforms to the NIST Privacy Framework. Map the program to NIST as you write it and Tennessee stops being a risk at zero marginal cost.

Deliverable: a dated, signed DPIA held on file. Not published. Produce it to a regulator on request — and note that in several states the AG can demand it, so write it as though it will be read adversarially.

subtasks.title: Set a quarterly review reminder for biometric legislation
subtasks.description:
This area moves faster than almost any other in US privacy. A snapshot decays in about six months.

WATCH LIST, in order of likely impact on us:
1. NEW YORK STATE — the New York Biometric Privacy Act has been introduced repeatedly and would substantially mirror BIPA INCLUDING A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION. If it passes, New York becomes an instant Tier 1 state and roughly doubles our national exposure overnight. This is the single most important thing on this list.
2. Further BIPA amendments and appellate decisions — the 2024 SB 2979 amendment (per-person rather than per-scan accrual, electronic signatures permitted) is still being interpreted by courts. Watch how 'same method of collection' gets construed; a narrow reading partially revives per-scan exposure.
3. Washington MHMDA litigation — whether courts accept that biometric data used purely for identity verification is 'consumer health data' when it reveals nothing about health. This is the open question that determines whether Washington is Tier 1 or a non-issue for us.
4. Maryland MODPA enforcement and any guidance on what 'strictly necessary' means. Currently undefined by regulators or courts. Also note the discretionary cure period SUNSETS APRIL 1 2027 — after that there is no cure safety net in Maryland.
5. Colorado HB 24-1130 enforcement, particularly on the prohibition against conditioning service on biometric consent, which is the provision that bites our signup flow hardest.
6. New comprehensive state privacy laws taking effect, and new biometric-specific bills. Several states have introduced BIPA-style bills WITH private rights of action; any one that passes changes the map materially.
7. FTC activity on biometrics under the May 2023 policy statement, especially any further algorithmic-disgorgement orders.

HOW TO DO THIS CHEAPLY IN 15 MINUTES A QUARTER: check the IAPP US State Privacy Legislation Tracker, skim one or two law-firm biometric-privacy roundups, and confirm nothing on the list above has moved. If something has, reopen the parent task rather than trying to patch it in here.

Also re-run the APPLICABILITY THRESHOLDS as we grow: the 35,000-consumer states (Connecticut, Rhode Island, Maryland, New Hampshire, Delaware) come into scope first and are the ones most often missed. Set a trigger to re-check when we pass 30,000 users in any single state.
